title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden: Drust Cycles – John Watson
content:
Guten morgen! We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. On this rainy Sunday morning, we’ve got a special feature from the Berlin-based Drust Cycles…

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2025 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

Konstantin Drust finally won the award for “Best Cargo Bike” at the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. The Berlin-based builder displayed two complete bicycles at his booth, which he shared with his apprentice Kata Rasch from Rasch Cycles (more on her later). With a whopping 100+ photos of these creations, we’re giving Drust its own showcase this year. Let’s check ’em out.

2026 Bespoked Dresden Drust Cargo

Mental Bikes for Mental People. Every few years, Konstantin likes to build himself a bike for Bespoked. This allows for a platform to display his talents and a canvas for experimentation. His bike this year displayed a wondrous front rack, which features a detachable low-rider mount.

Displayed with custom bags from his studio mate Gramm Tourpacking, Tine Heil selected a pastel palette to complement the peach colored frame, using orange highlights to create contrast with the bright blue rack. The panniers are featherlight. When we removed them for the photoshoot, they felt like feathers. “Do you like my troll? Putting the bottle in the pannier, right next to the bottle cages?”

Paired with two massive framebags, split by the diagatube that stiffens the frame, it’s a perfect collaboration between Gramm and Drust. Tine’s work really shines on Konstantin’s bikes.

“I just eyeballed it all…” Konstantin commented as he turned the front wheel, which elegantly clears the front lowriders, letting out a gleeful giggle. “It’s really fun to see it all work out in the end.”

Drust’s abilities are in full display on this bike. If you want to see where a builder or maker’s head is at, look at what they build for themselves. Konstantin tours and bike camps with his dog, so utilizing every available free space for extra camping items is crucial. There’s a low-slung rack cradle for extra items, right behind the front wheel’s fenders.

“For me, the detail I love is the matching Silca frame pump.” He commented, sitting back, proud of his work. The cable routing is another moment of pride in this bike full of impeccable detailing.

Compared to the Klunkargo Safari he built for me, the rake on this fork is less, creating a quicker, more nimble ride feel, perfect for pavement and hardpack touring. For some reason, this bike reminds me of a rolling piece of funky, mid-century furniture with beautiful lines and fabrics, which complement each other in an incredible way, void of ostentation.

Michael’s Drust Touring Bike

Last year, I documented Michael‘s Drust tourer with a beautiful tiger-striped, flame-kissed finish. This year, the returning customer donned a new look for himself along with a new bike. “I was going for sleazy uncle…” Michael joked as I asked him to lie in front of his new Drust 26″ tourer.

“I was sold on 24″ wheels, but then I started to panic that there weren’t enough tires on the market,” he lamented, “so we went with 26+ instead.” The bike, while not technically a mini velo, has a stance similar to the modern ATBs produced by brands like Crust and Stridsland. It’s nimble, capable, and cush. Just what Michael wanted.

“When I saw the quick-release Rinko dynamo routing on your bike, I had to spring for that detail on mine,” Michael continued, noting the stereo plug Drust offers in collaboration with Fern Cycles, popularized by Japanese tourers who must detach their bikes for Shinkansen transport.

For convenience of travel, the rear end collapses, and the seat stay binders can be bolted to the bosses on the downtube. This detail, along with the smaller diameter wheels, will allow Michael to transport the bike easily. He’s also using the MKS Allways pedals, which allow for quick and easy removal. As a photographer, these pedals refused to lie level with the crank arms due to their superb bearings. I had to have Michael rotate them to the correct position and fire off a high-speed burst to get the crank photos correct.

The client had Konstantin construct a front rack to hold the Outer Shell Rack Bag, with its leopard-print fabric, really complementing Michael’s garb and the bike’s finish. “We wanted the bike to look like a freshly poured Guinness,” he commented as I pored over the bike’s details. “They didn’t quite nail it, but I’m really happy with the final product.”

Konstantin’s front rack attaches directly to the frame, so the bike steers while the rack stays pointed forward. This takes a bit of problem-solving to achieve the correct height. “You have to clear the bag with your handlebars, and also be aware of the front light bracket not hitting the wheel when you cut the bars.” The bihawk-sporting builder commented.

On a personal note, it brings me great joy to document Drust Cycles’ work each year. I’ve gotten to know Konstantin Drust over the past few years, bought a bike for myself last year, and thoroughly enjoy my time spent with this wonderful human. We’ve got one more feature on the way this week, which will fall into our torrent of 2026 Bespoked Dresden coverage!

Til then, I must ask, which bike documented here would you want in your stable?
